excerpt: Clothes fade faster when heat, friction, harsh chemistry, and unnecessarily intensive cycles are combined. No trick stops all wear, but following care labels, separating unstable dyes, and reducing unnecessary heat exposure can preserve color for longer.
content_html:
Clothes fade faster when heat, friction, harsh chemistry, and unnecessarily intensive cycles are combined. No trick stops all wear, but following care labels, separating unstable dyes, and reducing unnecessary heat exposure can preserve color for longer.

Check care labels and separate unstable dyes

A new dark, red, or deeply dyed garment may release color during early washes. Wash it with similar colors and, when uncertain, test colorfastness in an inconspicuous area before combining it with light clothing.

Use the lowest temperature that still cleans effectively

Very hot water can accelerate dye loss and fiber wear when clothing does not need it. Choose cool or warm water when the care label and soil level allow, reserving higher temperatures for loads that genuinely require them.

Reduce friction on the visible surface

Turn jeans, printed shirts, and dark garments inside out before washing and do not overfill the drum. A suitable cycle with enough space reduces unnecessary rubbing between fabrics and against the machine.

Avoid excessive drying heat

High dryer heat can speed up a dull appearance and damage prints or heat-sensitive fibers. Dry at the setting allowed by the label and remove clothes when they are dry instead of extending the cycle by habit.
